item.title: LSZ president Ncube joins JSC, pledges to strengthen judicial independence
item.description: Gibson Mhaka Senior Reporter LAW Society of Zimbabwe (LSZ) president Mr Lison Ncube has pledged to contribute towards strengthening judicial independence, accountability and the efficient administration of justice following his appointment as one of the new commissioners of the Judicial Service Commission (JSC). Mr Ncube was sworn in by Chief Justice Elizabeth Gwaunza alongside Dr Noah Maringe, Mr Valentine Mutatu, Mr Bothwell Nyajeka and Mrs Alice Chipo Nyamugama, marking the beginning of a new six-year term for the constitutional body charged with promoting judicial independence and ensuring the effective administration of justice in Zimbabwe. His appointment comes only weeks after he and LSZ vice-president Ms Rachel Chibaya were elected to the Executive Council of the Southern African Development Community Lawyers’ Association (SADC-LA), a regional body representing law societies from across the SADC region. The twin appointments have further elevated Zimbabwe’s legal profession on both the national and regional stages, underscoring growing confidence in the country’s legal practitioners. Speaking after taking the oath of office, Mr Ncube described his appointment as both a privilege and a solemn responsibility, saying he was committed to advancing the constitutional mandate of the JSC. I am humbly honoured to have been appointed to serve on the Commission and it gives me great honour and pleasure to contribute to the JSC’s administrative mandate, as provided in Section 190 of the Constitution, which is to promote and facilitate the independence and accountability of the judiciary and maintain the administration of justice in Zimbabwe in a high state of effectiveness, efficiency and transparency, he said. I look forward to adding value to a JSC whose vision is to deliver world-class justice. Section 190 of the Constitution mandates the JSC to safeguard the independence of the judiciary while ensuring that Zimbabwe’s justice delivery system remains effective, efficient and transparent. Mr Ncube said his appointment to the Commission, coming on the heels of his recent election to the SADC-LA Executive Council in Maputo, Mozambique, reflected growing regional confidence in Zimbabwe’s legal profession. The appointment also comes in the wake of my recent election to the SADC-LA Executive Council, a body comprising 15 law societies in the SADC region. This regional appointment places Zimbabwe on the map and is testament to the belief that the region has in the competence and capabilities of the legal profession in Zimbabwe, he said. He said the recent appointments were a reflection of the progress made by the LSZ during his tenure as president. These recent appointments are testament to the hard work and dedication that I humbly believe I have put towards the legal profession in Zimbabwe during my tenure as President of the Law Society. Mr Ncube said Zimbabwe continued to produce legal practitioners whose expertise was receiving recognition beyond the country’s borders. This regional elevation is a clear indication that the future remains bright. Zimbabwe continues to produce leaders of distinction whose capabilities are recognised and respected throughout the region. The LSZ has, without doubt, maintained a strong presence and its efforts have not gone unnoticed, he said. He said the legal profession was becoming increasingly important as Southern Africa experienced deeper regional integration and expanding cross-border investment. At a time when the legal landscape is rapidly evolving, marked by increasing regional integration and the expansion of cross-border trade, the role of the legal profession becomes even more critical. The recent election to this regional body underscores the pivotal role of the Bar in shaping and advancing the legal profession in Zimbabwe, said Mr Ncube. He paid tribute to former LSZ leaders whose stewardship helped position Zimbabwe’s legal profession among the most respected in the region. It also reflects a continuation of the legacy built by esteemed figures such as Mrs Vimbai Nyemba, Lloyd Mhishi, Josphat Tshuma and the late Sternford Moyo, among many others, whose leadership elevated the LSZ to remarkable heights, culminating in Mr Moyo’s appointment as President of the International Bar Association. Mr Ncube said Zimbabwe’s growing attractiveness as an investment destination required a robust, internationally respected legal profession capable of supporting economic development. As Zimbabwe positions itself as open for business, with growing international interest in sectors such as mining and commercial transactions, there is an urgent need for a legal profession that is well-integrated, dynamic and globally respected. “The Government of Zimbabwe also needs a pool of lawyers to consult from that is well-engaged internationally and regionally respected. This will ensure that local practitioners remain competitive and are not sidelined in favour of foreign law firms. Hence, this is a big step for Zimbabwe as a whole, he said. Legal analysts said Mr Ncube’s appointment to the JSC, together with his election to the SADC-LA Executive Council, reflects the increasing prominence of Zimbabwe’s legal profession within regional legal institutions at a time when the country continues to strengthen the rule of law, judicial efficiency and investor confidence. JSC plays a central role in supporting the independence of the judiciary, overseeing the administration of the courts and ensuring that Zimbabwe’s justice delivery system continues to operate effectively in line with constitutional principles. (via The Sunday News) #Zimbabwe #ZimbabweNews
item.dc:creator: The Sunday News

item.title: Bad weather delays arrival of Nothabo, daughters’ bodies
item.description: Bongani Ndlovu, THE arrival of the bodies of Zandile Nothabo Khumalo and her two daughters, Natalie and Nala, in Zimbabwe has been delayed after bad weather disrupted their journey from the United Kingdom, forcing the aircraft carrying them to divert before reaching its scheduled transit destination in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. The diversion meant the bodies missed their connecting Ethiopian Airlines flight to Bulawayo on Sunday morning, delaying their return home by several hours. Family spokesperson Mr Khumalo said the aircraft was unable to land in Addis Ababa because of adverse weather conditions and was instead diverted to Djibouti. The flight from the United Kingdom failed to land in Addis Ababa because of bad weather. It had to divert to Djibouti, and because of that, they missed the connecting flight from Addis Ababa to Bulawayo, he said. Mr Khumalo said the bodies are now expected to arrive at Robert Gabriel Mugabe International Airport in Harare around midnight before being transported by road to Bulawayo. Despite the delay, he said all funeral arrangements remain unchanged. The bodies are expected to briefly pass through the Khumalo family home in Gwabalanda before a funeral service at the Brethren in Christ Church in Lobengula. Thereafter, Nothabo and her daughters will be laid to rest side by side at Old Luveve Cemetery on Tuesday. Mr Khumalo said the repatriation marks an important step towards bringing closure to the grieving family after weeks of mourning and logistical arrangements involving authorities in Zimbabwe and the United Kingdom. Earlier, he said the family had been relieved after British authorities approved the repatriation of Natalie and Nala, who were born in the United Kingdom, allowing them to be buried alongside their mother in Zimbabwe. It was our worry as a family that as the children were born in the United Kingdom, but the authorities were very understanding about burying the two children along with their mother in Zimbabwe, rather than separating them. Zandile’s mother and father are comforted about this development as this had been their heart’s desire that their grandchildren and daughter be buried in Zimbabwe as a way for them to get closure, he said. Nothabo (32) and her daughters were found dead at their home in Great Denham, Bedfordshire, on July 3 in a case that shocked both Zimbabweans and the wider British community. Her husband and the children’s father, Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma, a Zimbabwean-born British citizen, was later arrested in Johannesburg, South Africa. He is still in custody as the United Kingdom authorities pursue his extradition to face three counts of murder. The deaths triggered an outpouring of grief and solidarity from Zimbabweans at home and abroad, with individuals, community organisations and well-wishers mobilising financial and logistical support to ensure the three are brought home for burial. Their funeral is expected to draw mourners from across the country, as family, friends and members of the community bid farewell to a mother and her two young daughters whose tragic deaths have touched many people in Zimbabwe and beyond. (via The Sunday News) #Zimbabwe #ZimbabweNews
